title: Keeping Score
hook: The revenue slide can wait until Erin shows the lead-action score everyone avoided.
counterintuition: Scorekeeping gets weak when it becomes a report card for self-worth. The useful score is visible feedback: it tells you whether the promised actions happened soon enough to adjust the week.
tryThisNow: Choose one lead action and mark a simple weekly score: planned count, completed count, and what must change next week.
keyTakeaway: Track execution visibly enough that the score tells you what to adjust before the cycle is over. The standard is visible action, not a better-sounding intention.

breakdown.fastRead: A score sheet glows above the sales huddle. Effort can feel strong while the lead actions are weak. Keeping Score makes drift visible before it turns into a story. A useful score is not a report card for self-worth. It is feedback. It tells the team what happened soon enough to change what happens next. The huddle should leave with one clear adjustment, not just a cleaner slide about last week.

examples.title: Erin shows the action score first

planSpec.audience: a practitioner in sales team score huddle who needs the chapter move under real pressure
planSpec.stakes: the visible result will slip while everyone can still explain the effort
planSpec.requiredBeat: Erin posts the lead-action score before talking about revenue.

examples.scenario: A score sheet glows above the sales huddle before the revenue slide appears. Erin must decide whether to open with closed deals or with the promised lead actions: twenty renewal calls planned, thirteen completed, four follow-ups missed. She posts the execution score first and asks what changes before Friday.
examples.whatToDo: Put the lead-action score ahead of the result number, then choose one adjustment while there is still time to act.
examples.whyItMatters: Revenue arrives late. Erin keeps the team honest by scoring the behavior they can still change.

examples.title: Harriet counts calls, not atmosphere

planSpec.audience: a decision-maker in calligraphy workshop enrollment choosing whether to protect execution or drift
planSpec.stakes: the next 12 weeks will inherit a soft plan unless the decision is made now
planSpec.requiredBeat: Harriet tracks enrollment calls instead of how busy the workshop felt.

examples.scenario: "Busy is not a score," Harriet says, with ink bottles lined across the workshop table. The enrollment push feels alive, but she must decide whether to count compliments from visitors or the outbound calls that were actually made to past students.
examples.whatToDo: Score the enrollment calls, deposits, and follow-ups separately from the energy in the room.
examples.whyItMatters: The workshop can feel active while the plan starves. Harriet uses visible feedback to separate motion from execution.

examples.title: Isabel marks the cases honestly

planSpec.audience: a team lead in public benefits casework who needs visible proof before the week softens
planSpec.stakes: the team will mistake motion for progress if the proof stays hidden
planSpec.requiredBeat: Isabel marks completed benefit cases against the plan.

examples.scenario: You can hear the phone ringing beside a stack of public benefits files, and every call sounds urgent. Isabel must decide whether to report total contacts or mark completed cases against the weekly plan. The reveal is uncomfortable: the team answered plenty of calls and completed too few benefit decisions.
examples.whatToDo: Mark completed cases against the plan, then use the gap to change intake blocks before the week ends.
examples.whyItMatters: A score changes behavior because it makes drift visible before drift can become a story. Isabel makes the truth useful rather than punishing.

examples.title: Juliet finds the lab bottleneck

planSpec.audience: a reflective operator in medical lab sample turnaround reading last week's failure as evidence
planSpec.stakes: a repeat failure will be explained away instead of corrected
planSpec.requiredBeat: Juliet shows sample turnaround by day and changes staffing.

examples.scenario: It took Juliet one Friday chart under blue lab lights to stop blaming the whole week. Sample turnaround was fine Monday through Wednesday and broke after 2 p.m. Thursday. She brings the daily score to staffing review and moves a technician into the late queue before the next batch arrives.
examples.whatToDo: Show turnaround by day and time block, then change staffing where the score shows the actual break.
examples.whyItMatters: Juliet avoids a vague correction. The score points to the point of failure, so the adjustment can be precise.

examples.title: Leila scores the route checks

planSpec.audience: a reader in park maintenance crew board comparing intention before the move with proof after it
planSpec.stakes: the work will stay aspirational unless the action changes in the room
planSpec.requiredBeat: Leila counts completed route checks before praising effort.

examples.scenario: At 6:30 a.m. in the parks garage, Leila counts salt bags stacked by the door. As crew lead, she must decide whether to praise storm effort first or score completed route checks and missed hazards.
examples.whatToDo: Score completed route checks and missed hazards before praising effort.
examples.whyItMatters: Leila keeps scorekeeping out of personality. The board turns effort into operational feedback the crew can use.

examples.title: Paige makes builds measurable

planSpec.audience: two colleagues in Helsinki mobile games studio forcing the commitment into plain speech
planSpec.stakes: a public promise will dissolve unless someone names the proof and owner
planSpec.requiredBeat: Paige scores test builds against the sprint commitment.

examples.scenario: Which build counts as done enough to score? Paige asks in the Helsinki mobile games studio, test phone blinking beside the release notes. The team must decide whether to celebrate build volume or score each test build against the sprint commitment: crash-free launch, tutorial completion, and upload time.
examples.whatToDo: Define the build score before the sprint review, then mark every test build against the same commitment.
examples.whyItMatters: Paige prevents measurement theater. A useful score changes the next build instead of decorating the review.
